## 1. Skill vs MCP vs plugin vs others
| Need | Use |
|---|---|
| Always-true facts (conventions, commands, "never X") | `AGENTS.md` / always-on rule (CLAUDE.md <200 lines; Codex truncates at 32 KiB) |
| Procedure needed sometimes | Skill |
| Auth, secrets, live data, external writes, persistent state | MCP server, paired with a skill that teaches its use |
| Must happen every time (enforcement) | Hook (an instruction is a request, a hook is enforcement; costs no context) |
| Side task that floods context / parallel read-only work | Subagent |
| Ship to other repos or teams | Plugin (bundle; namespaced `/plugin:skill`) |
| Prompt you keep retyping | Skill with `disable-model-invocation: true` (commands merged into skills) |
- Vercel evals: an 8 KB docs index in AGENTS.md passed 100%; the skill was never opened in 56% of runs (79% max when told explicitly). So: put an index of pointers in always-on context, and use skills for action-specific workflows.
- If the agent has a shell and no auth is needed, a CLI with good `--help` plus a skill often beats an MCP server.
- MCP SEP-2640 (Final, 2026-04): MCP servers can serve skills (`skills/list`, `skills/get`); per-skill user approval before any code runs; re-approval when the content hash changes.

## 2. When to split a skill
- Limits: SKILL.md <500 lines and ~5k tokens; name + description ~100 tokens; description ≤1,024 chars (spec); Claude Code truncates description + `when_to_use` at 1,536 chars.
- The listing budget is the binding constraint: Claude Code 1% of context, Codex 2% (8k chars if unknown). On overflow, the least-used descriptions are cut first. Front-load trigger words.
- **Split when:** distinct triggers or intents; different side effects (read-only analysis vs `/apply`); different runtime needs (`compatibility`); activation is imprecise because scope is too broad.
- **Don't split when:** variants are mutually exclusive (AWS/GCP/Azure → one workflow + `references/<p>.md`); the parts always load together (risk of conflicting instructions); overlap can be fixed by tightening both descriptions first.
- References: one level deep (nested files get partially read, e.g. `head -100`); add a table of contents if >100 lines; state *when* to load each ("read X if API returns non-200").
- Router skill: chooses only, then points to refs, sibling skills, or subagents.
- Shared content: duplicate it or use a plugin-level script; avoid cross-skill relative paths (paths resolve from the skill root).
- Use unique names; never rely on shadowing (precedence differs: Claude managed>user>project, Gemini workspace>user, Codex shows both).

## 4. Subagents
- Use for: breadth research fan-out, reading many files or logs when only a summary is needed, independent review (sees the diff only, none of the author's context), parallel read-only work.
- Avoid when: phases share heavy context, the task needs back-and-forth, latency matters, or it's a quick targeted change.
- Cost: ~15× the *total billed tokens* of one chat exchange (a single agent loop is ~4×), so multi-agent ≈ 3–4× a single agent. This is not the size of the main context: the main context shrinks, because it only receives summaries. Where the tokens come from: (1) every subagent re-pays the fixed prefix (system prompt + tool schemas + brief, often 10–30k tokens); (2) each agent turn resends the whole growing transcript, so a 20-turn loop bills roughly the sum of every intermediate context (~quadratic in turns); (3) parallel workers each read their own sources, with overlap; (4) the lead reads the summaries, plus synthesis and retries. Example: 5 workers × 20 turns × ~40k average context ≈ 4M input tokens, vs ~0.25M for one chat. Prompt caching makes repeated prefixes ~90% cheaper but doesn't remove them. Token usage explained 80% of performance variance in Anthropic's research system (+90% vs single Opus), so you are buying quality with tokens; only do it when the task is worth it.
- Consensus (Anthropic + Cognition 2026): writes stay single-threaded; extra agents contribute intelligence, not actions. Swarms are "a distraction".
- Effort scaling: 1 agent / 3–10 calls for simple tasks; 2–4 subagents for comparisons; >10 only for complex research.
- Subagents write artifacts to disk and return a path + a 1–2k-token summary (avoids a "game of telephone").
- Context sharing: workers/consultants get a fork of full context; reviewers get none.
- Cap depth (Claude default 3); read-only reviewers get no Agent tool. Subagents may not inherit skills (Deep Agents doesn't; Claude `skills:` preloads them).

## 16. Side-effect gating (added)
| Host | Mechanism | Semantics |
|---|---|---|
| Claude Code | `disable-model-invocation: true` | No auto-load; description not in context; can't be preloaded into subagents. Use for deploy, commit, send. |
| Claude Code | `user-invocable: false` | Hidden from `/` menu; only the model can invoke it. |
| Claude Code | `allowed-tools` / `disallowed-tools`; permission rules `Skill(name)` | `allowed-tools` pre-approves for one turn and restricts nothing. Deny via `disallowed-tools` or rules. `allowManagedPermissionRulesOnly` ignores skill grants. |
| Claude Code | settings `skillOverrides` (`on`/`name-only`/`user-invocable-only`/`off`) | Does NOT apply to plugin skills. |
| Cursor | `disable-model-invocation: true` | Only included when you type `/skill-name`. |
| Codex | `agents/openai.yaml` `policy.allow_implicit_invocation: false` (default true) | Explicit `$skill` only. |
| Gemini CLI | consent prompt on `activate_skill`; policy `ask_user` | Extensions can't self-approve (`allow` and yolo ignored). |
| Copilot | `allowed-tools` | Skips confirmation; don't pre-approve shell/bash. |
| MCP SEP-2640 | per-skill approval bound to sha256 digests | Changed digest → re-approval. |
- Rules: anything irreversible is user-invoked only; scripts need `--confirm` + `--dry-run`; destructive steps outside the approved plan → stop and ask.
